To understand how a refrigerator maintains the cold temperature of our food, we must first look at the concept of a refrigeration cycle, which is essentially a closed loop of heat transfer. Unlike a simple freezer that just removes heat, a refrigerator uses a cycle similar to how a car engine works, but in reverse. The core of this system is the compressor, which acts as the heart of the refrigeration process. When the compressor runs, it compresses a low-pressure gas of refrigerant, increasing its pressure and temperature. This high-pressure gas then travels to the condenser, where it releases its heat into the surrounding environment, typically a cool room or the outside of the fridge.

The next component to consider is the expansion valve. As the high-pressure gas moves through the system, it passes through an expansion valve, which allows the pressure to drop significantly. This sudden drop in pressure causes the temperature of the gas to plummet. This is the crucial moment where the cold air is created. The cold, low-pressure gas then flows into the evaporator, which is usually a coil located inside the walls of the refrigerator.
